newsitem.title: CHINA: China's dynamic source of funds.
newsitem.headline: China's dynamic source of funds.

text.p: China's ambitious drive towards modernisation will require the funnelling of vast amounts of capital into key areas in coming years, and its dynamic red chips are destined to be an important channel.
These China-backed companies, based and listed in Hong Kong, are the darlings of the Hong Kong stock market and raised more than US$3 billion during the first half of 1997.
"Equity funding is a relatively new feature for attracting foreign capital into China," said Benny Chiu, research manager at Hongkong Bank.

"The most important way of attracting foreign capital into China is still through foreign loans and foreign direct investment, but this new means of raising funds through the equity markets is developing fast," he added.

Hong Kong boasts the seventh largest stock market in the world and is more attractive than Chinese domestic markets for raising funds. "The issue is that you are gaining access to a much deeper and much more international capital market," said Abhijit Chakraborrti, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers.
CHINESE MARKETS UNABLE TO MEET DEMAND FOR CAPITAL
With huge financing needs on the mainland, particularly in the infrastructure sector, analysts said China's domestic markets would be unable to satisfy the demand for capital.

Meanwhile actual foreign investment in China is expected to slip to around US$40 billion this year from a record US$42.35 billion in 1996, and then hover at around US$30 billion a year between 1998 and 2000, according to Chinese economists.

Johnson Cheung, an analyst at Goldman Sachs, said red chips and H-shares -- shares of China-incorporated companies listed in Hong Kong -- raised US$4 billion in the first half of 1997, equivalent to about 10 percent of foreign direct investment.
"The ratio could go up to 20 percent," he said.
RED CHIPS ARE EFFICIENT USERS OF CASH

Cheung said most of the funds raised by red chip companies was destined for investments in China and red chips were effective users of cash, since listings in Hong Kong enhanced transparency and made them accountable to minority shareholders.
"If you raise money through the equity market, you have to prepare the companies so that they are ready to absorb this sort of capital. You have to do a lot of restructuring," added Chiu.

More flexible than China's lumbering H-share companies, red chips were more effective in adjusting to the changing economic environment, said Cheung. "They can adapt their asset injection strategies to complement China's national policies."

"Currently most red chips are focusing on infrastructure, particularly toll roads, because of investors' demand for projects with strong cash flow, but this also fits in with the government's needs for more infrastructure investment," he said.

China has said it needs US$65 billion for highway construction over the next five years. Chinese highway operators have carried out initial public offerings in Hong Kong and red chips have raised money through share issues.
Shanghai Industrial Holdings, the investment arm of the Shanghai municipal government, raised HK$4.8 billion through a share issue in April to buy two roads in Shanghai.
China Merchants Holdings (International) Co Ltd also raised HK$3.86 billion in April to fund the purchase of toll road and container businesses.
The development of Chinese ports is also a priority, with China hoping to develop trade with increased shipping activity.

Red chip COSCO Pacific Ltd, indirectly controlled by China Ocean Shipping (Group) Co, has been a favoured vehicle and raised HK$1.2 billion in a share placement in March to fund port acquisitions and the expansion of Chinese terminals and container manufacturing plants.
"Basically what China is doing is modernising," said Howard Gorges, vice chairman at South China Holdings.
"It helps get more capital into the business faster than the sate would be able to provide it," he said.

China is also due to raise funds for its airline industry in the second half of 1997 with the Hong Kong listings of China Southern Airlines and China National Aviation Corp, an airline group controlled by China's Civil Aviation Administration.
TELECOMMUNICATIONS AND BANKING SENSITIVE AREAS

The first listing of a major China-backed telecommunications operator is expected by year-end, with the massive and much awaited initial public offering of China Telecom, a company backed by China's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications.
The offering is expected to be the biggest ever Hong Kong listing of a China-backed company, raising about US$6 billion.

China Telecom is due to pay for Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd shares with the proceeds, following an agreement last month under which Cable and Wireless Plc said it would sell Hongkong Telecom shares to China Telecom.
Analysts said proceeds should also be ploughed into China's fixed line and mobile networks.
"The setting up of a separate vehicle for raising funds for the development of the telecom business on the mainland is an important step forward," said Chakrabortti.

But analysts said that with foreign companies restricted from operating in China's telecommunications market, Chinese authorities would keep tight control on listings in the area and they may be slow in coming to the market.
"Banking is even more sensitive," added Ken Chan, senior economist at Nikko Research Center (Hong Kong).
"Foreign banks can only operate in limited areas and I don't think the central bank wants to lose control." Chan said red chips were unlikely to be a source of funds to develop the banking industry.
"At some future date they may well list a bank but I don't think they are ready yet," said Gorges. "It is politically sensitive and also very subject to regulation."
But China's recent approval of red chip China Everbright-IHD Pacific Ltd's acquisition of a stake in sister company Everbright Bank of China was an encouraging sign, analysts said.

"This kind of listing -- which allows a wider source of funding for the Chinese banking system -- fits in with the genuine strategy of the Chinese authorities," said Raymond Lee, banking analyst at Lehman Brothers.
"The question is when will the appropriate timing be."
China has said that it will tighten controls on red chip listings and injections of mainland assets into the firms but analysts said they expected major red chips to remain active.
"The process will be slowed down if the government issues guidelines but longer term, it is a very efficient way for China to raise funds in the priority sectors," said Chan.
